Three or more generations living together or in close contact; more common in pre-industrial and collectivist societies.

walkthroughs.body_html:
Families — a core area of GCSE Sociology.

Working through it builds the schema you need: the key terms, how they connect, and how to use them together.

Families brings together several ideas you need to use as a set, not in isolation.

Lock in the vocabulary first, then practise pulling the ideas together to answer real questions.

Use the activities in this adventure to build familiarity with Families.

Practise vocabulary, calculations and free-text questions to lock in the learning.

mcqs.q: Who argued the family had become symmetrical in 1973?
options: Murdock
Parsons
Young and Willmott
Oakley

mcqs.q: Murdock (1949) identified how many family functions?

options: A reconstituted family is one that has been put back together after divorce.
A family formed when partners with children from previous relationships come together — a 'blended' or step-family — one of several family forms recognised in family diversity literature.
Wealthy elites secretly control society.
A reconstituted family is a family living in temporary housing.
Weber's three dimensions are upper, middle and working class.
Wealthy elites secretly control society.
A distinct group develops a culture of welfare dependency and anti-social behaviour.
All working-class people are an underclass.

mcqs.q: What are Weber's three dimensions of stratification?
options: Class (economic position in markets), status (social honour/prestige), and party (organised power) — Weber argued these can vary independently, unlike Marx's economic-determinism view.
Weber agreed with Marx that class is purely economic.
Wealthy elites secretly control society.
Weber's three dimensions are upper, middle and working class.
